turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Many Japanese Chardonnay makers now talk about bâtonnage. What is that?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Bâtonnage is a French word. In English, we usually say lees stirring. After fermentation, dead yeast cells sink to the bottom of the barrel. These are called the lees.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And you stir them back into the wine?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. The winemaker puts a stick into the barrel and gently mixes the lees through the wine, maybe once or twice a week, for some months.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Why would you want dead yeast in your wine?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Because they slowly break down and release interesting compounds. This process is called yeast autolysis. It gives the wine a rounder, creamier texture, and flavors like bread, nuts or biscuits.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Is it especially useful in Japan?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It can be. In some years, Japanese Chardonnay can feel a little light, because of rain or cool weather. Lees stirring adds body and a gentle savory quality, a bit like umami. It also helps protect the wine from oxygen.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes. If you stir too much, the wine can become heavy and lose its freshness. It's about balance. The best winemakers taste the wine often and decide carefully when to stop.
